labels.name: Interpreter or Parser Injection
labels.description: Attacker-controlled data changes the grammar, executable structure, or directives consumed by an interpreter or parser instead of remaining a literal value. Evidence must identify the interpreted context and how input crosses its syntax boundary; malformed data that only crashes a parser, object reconstruction, and path selection are outside this family.

labels.name: Query-Language Injection
labels.description: Interpreter injection in which untrusted data changes a database, directory, or document-query expression. Evidence must show alteration of query operators, predicates, or statement structure; an attacker supplying an unexpected but still literal query value is not sufficient.

labels.name: Process Invocation Injection
labels.description: Interpreter or parser injection in which attacker-controlled input changes an operating-system process invocation. Evidence must show influence over shell syntax or the invoked program's argument grammar; selecting an already authorized fixed action without changing invocation structure is an authorization issue instead.

labels.name: Dynamic Code Evaluation
labels.description: Interpreter injection in which attacker-controlled text is evaluated as program code, an expression language, or a server-side template. Evidence must establish the input-to-evaluator transition; code execution as an impact of memory corruption, deserialization, or command injection does not establish this family.

labels.name: Browser Document Injection
labels.description: Interpreter or parser injection in which attacker-controlled markup or script-capable content changes a browser-consumed document. Evidence must show unsafe insertion into an HTML, SVG, or equivalent browser parsing context; server-side templates and redirects are outside this family.

labels.name: Filesystem Resource Boundary Violation
labels.description: Attacker-controlled names, paths, archive entries, or filesystem links resolve to a file or directory outside the resource set intended for an operation. Evidence must show unauthorized filesystem target selection; object identifiers, network destinations, and merely dangerous uploaded content use other families.

labels.name: Path Traversal
labels.description: A filesystem resource boundary violation in which crafted path components, absolute paths, encoded separators, or normalization discrepancies escape an intended directory. Evidence must establish the resolved filesystem scope; accessing another database object by identifier without a permission check is an authorization failure, not path traversal.

labels.name: Improper Filesystem Link Resolution
labels.description: A filesystem resource boundary violation in which a symbolic link, hard link, junction, mount, or equivalent reference resolves an operation to an unauthorized target. Evidence must identify link following or replacement; lexical or normalization-based escapes belong to PathTraversal.

labels.name: Unsafe Structured-Data Interpretation
labels.description: Attacker-controlled structured data is interpreted with object, reference, binding, or graph capabilities beyond the intended data-only contract. Evidence must identify the unsafe structured-data feature; ordinary parser crashes, query injection, and path traversal are outside this family.

labels.name: Deserialization of Untrusted Data
labels.description: Unsafe structured-data interpretation in which attacker-controlled serialized data reconstructs objects without adequate type or behavior restrictions, enabling gadget invocation, unsafe construction, or security-sensitive state changes. Parsing plain data without object reconstruction is not sufficient.

labels.name: XML External Entity Processing
labels.description: Unsafe structured-data interpretation in which an XML parser processes attacker-controlled external entity declarations or references. Evidence must establish entity resolution; XML deserialization gadgets and XPath expression changes use their respective sibling families.

labels.name: Prototype Pollution
labels.description: Unsafe structured-data interpretation in which attacker-controlled properties modify a shared prototype or inheritance object, causing later lookups to inherit unauthorized values or behavior. Changing only one ordinary object's permitted fields is not prototype pollution.

labels.name: Unsafe Mass Assignment
labels.description: Unsafe structured-data interpretation in which a framework binds untrusted fields to an object without an allowlist and thereby permits security-sensitive properties that are not externally writable. A correctly bound identifier followed by a missing permission check is ImproperAuthorization instead.

labels.name: Network Destination Control
labels.description: Attacker-controlled network identifiers determine an unintended network destination or routing authority for a request, redirect, backend selection, or security-sensitive absolute URL. Evidence must trace input to that destination or authority; selecting a filesystem resource or injecting protocol syntax belongs elsewhere.

labels.name: Server-Side Request Forgery
labels.description: Network destination control in which attacker input makes the vulnerable server issue a request to an unintended resource using the server's network position, identity, or credentials. An open redirect that only directs the user's client is not SSRF.

labels.name: Unvalidated Redirect
labels.description: Network destination control in which attacker-supplied destination data makes an application redirect a user's client to an unintended location without adequate destination validation. Server-originated fetching is SSRF, and host-controlled security links are HostHeaderInjection.

labels.name: Host Header Injection
labels.description: Network destination control in which an untrusted HTTP Host or forwarded-host value determines an unintended routing authority, backend, or security-sensitive absolute URL such as a password-reset link. Evidence must trace the untrusted host value to that destination or authority, not merely show acceptance of an unusual header.

labels.name: Unsafe File Upload Acceptance
labels.description: An upload feature accepts attacker-controlled file content contrary to its intended content policy or trust boundary. Evidence must concern what file content the feature accepts; missing permission to invoke the upload, filesystem destination traversal, and resource-size abuse are separate mechanisms.

labels.name: Dangerous File-Type Upload
labels.description: Unsafe file upload acceptance in which type or content validation permits executable, active, or otherwise dangerous content that the surrounding deployment will interpret or serve unsafely. Evidence must support the dangerous processing context, not merely the ability to store an arbitrary inert file.

labels.name: Identity and Access-Control Failure
labels.description: The system fails to establish a principal, bind an authenticated session, authorize an action or resource, or verify the legitimacy of an authority-bearing request. Evidence must identify the failed access decision; obtaining privileges only as an impact of another mechanism is not enough.

labels.name: Authentication Failure
labels.description: An identity and access-control failure in which the system grants or recovers an authenticated identity without sufficient proof that the requester is entitled to that identity. Evidence must concern identity establishment rather than permission for one operation; predictable session identifiers and cryptographic key-generation defects use their dedicated branches unless authentication logic also fails independently.

labels.name: Authenticated Session Management Failure
labels.description: An identity and access-control failure in the creation, binding, rotation, lifetime, or invalidation of a session identifier after identity proof. Evidence must concern authenticated session state; bearer tokens for one-time recovery or invitations are not sessions.

labels.name: Improper Action or Resource Authorization
labels.description: An identity and access-control failure in which a security-sensitive action or resource lacks an effective permission check or is evaluated against the wrong principal, action, resource, or context. This includes missing function-level checks; accepting or forging an authenticated identity is a distinct authentication failure when separately established.

labels.name: Authority-Bearing Request Validation Failure
labels.description: An identity and access-control failure in which a request carries otherwise valid ambient or delegated authority but the application fails to establish its intended origin, approval, or freshness. This is distinct from identity authentication and from a missing permission check on the requested action.

labels.name: Memory Safety Violation
labels.description: The implementation accesses or manages storage outside the bounds, lifetime, initialization, pointer-validity, or object-type rules of a memory-unsafe runtime. Evidence must identify an invalid memory operation or an authoritative memory-safety diagnosis; a managed exception, parser rejection, or denial-of-service impact alone is insufficient.

labels.name: Spatial Memory Safety Violation
labels.description: A memory safety violation in which a read or write targets bytes outside the valid bounds of the object or region authorized for that operation. Evidence must support an object boundary violation; invalid lifetime and incompatible object type have separate branches.

labels.name: Uninitialized Memory Read
labels.description: A memory safety violation in which the program reads bytes or fields that have not been initialized for the current object or operation. Evidence must establish the read of indeterminate or residual contents; a deliberately null pointer and stale freed storage use other labels.

labels.name: Temporal Memory Safety Violation
labels.description: A memory safety violation caused by accessing, releasing, or reusing a native allocation or object outside its valid lifetime. Evidence must establish allocation or ownership misuse involving memory; an object accessed with the wrong type but valid lifetime is TypeConfusion.

labels.name: Memory Object Type Confusion
labels.description: A memory safety violation in which native storage is treated as an incompatible object type or layout, causing unsafe field, method, element, or variant access. Evidence must support incompatible representation assumptions; ordinary data-type validation errors in memory-safe code are excluded.

labels.name: Null Pointer Dereference
labels.description: A memory safety violation in which native or other memory-unsafe code dereferences a null pointer because a required object or error state was not checked. Evidence must identify the invalid pointer dereference; a managed-language null-reference exception or denial-of-service impact alone is insufficient.

labels.name: Resource Management Failure
labels.description: The defining defect violates a finite-resource bound, release obligation, or progress guarantee under attacker-reachable conditions. Evidence must identify the resource rule that fails; a crash caused by injection or invalid memory access is not independently a resource-management mechanism.

labels.name: Uncontrolled Resource Consumption
labels.description: A resource management failure in which attacker-triggered work or state consumes CPU, memory, bandwidth, processes, or requests without an effective per-operation, per-client, or global bound. Evidence must identify the missing bound or amplification mechanism, not only service unavailability.

labels.name: Resource Release Failure
labels.description: A resource management failure in which resources acquired for completed, cancelled, or failed operations are not released and accumulate across operations. Evidence must establish retention beyond the intended lifecycle; one oversized allocation belongs to ResourceConsumption.

labels.name: Concurrency Progress Failure
labels.description: A resource management failure in which concurrent actors cannot make progress because locking or coordination rules permit a stable non-progress state. Evidence must establish a concurrency relationship; slow work or resource exhaustion without blocked actors is outside this branch.

labels.name: Cryptographic Protection Failure
labels.description: A security control fails because of cryptographic primitive selection, key management, randomness, nonce handling, or peer-certificate validation. Evidence must identify the failed cryptographic property; plaintext exposure without an intended cryptographic control does not by itself satisfy this label.

labels.name: Unsafe Cryptographic Algorithm Selection
labels.description: A cryptographic protection failure caused by choosing a primitive, mode, digest, or key size that cannot provide the claimed property in the stated threat model. Evidence must identify the selected construction and its inadequacy; implementation bugs with a sound selection belong elsewhere.

labels.name: Cryptographic Key Management Failure
labels.description: A cryptographic protection failure in key generation, storage, separation, distribution, rotation, or reuse rather than primitive selection. Evidence must concern secret key material; passwords and session identifiers are not cryptographic keys merely because they are secrets.

labels.name: Cryptographic Randomness or Nonce Failure
labels.description: A cryptographic protection failure caused by predictable, biased, repeated, or insufficiently large random values, nonces, initialization vectors, salts, or non-session security tokens. Predictable authenticated session identifiers are session-management failures and do not by themselves satisfy this label.

labels.name: Certificate and Peer Validation Failure
labels.description: A cryptographic protection failure in which a secure-channel client or verifier does not correctly validate the presented certificate chain, trust anchor, signature, constraints, validity, or peer identity. Evidence must concern certificate-based peer authentication, not application login.
